tldr: The authors propose CS-Pi, a new sampling method for pretrained flow policies that satisfies safety constraints—like unseen obstacles—strictly at inference time while preserving natural, plausible behaviors. By looping projection to the safe set with partial renoising scaled to the displacement, CS-Pi achieves an 81% safe success rate on a shelf pick-and-place task and 55% on a real robot.
hero_caption: Overview of flow policy generation under test-time safety constraints. Given diverse behavioral modes in a pretrained model (left), when a novel constraint like an obstacle is imposed at deployment (center), CS-Pi selectively samples actions that are both inside the safe region (Safe) and plausible under the policy distribution (right).
overview:
Recently, robot policies based on flow matching and diffusion models have become capable of learning versatile skills from large demonstration datasets. However, it is impossible for training data to cover every real-world situation. For example, even in a routine drawer-opening task, a robot might encounter a spur-of-the-moment safety constraint, such as dodging a wine glass that was placed nearby. Retraining the policy every time a new constraint appears is impractical, so constraints must be satisfied strictly at inference time during deployment.

The dominant existing approach, gradient guidance, steers the denoising trajectory using the gradient of a cost function during intermediate steps. However, intermediate noisy states lack a determined clean action. When the policy is torn between passing left or right around an obstacle, this approach takes their average, creating a critical flaw where the robot heads straight into the obstacle. Meanwhile, projection forcibly pushes generated actions into the safe set; while fast, it breaks the smoothness and task intent learned by the policy. Rejection sampling preserves naturalness by redrawing until an action is safe, but it becomes computationally intractable when safe actions are rare.

To solve this, the authors developed CS-Pi, combining the efficiency of projection with the plausibility of rejection sampling. It repeats a draw-project-renoise loop: projecting the generated action onto the safe set, re-adding an amount of noise scaled to how far it moved, and running the policy's denoising process again. This converges toward safe actions without restarting completely from scratch, all while preserving the policy's plausible behaviors. In both simulations and real-world experiments on a Franka arm, CS-Pi demonstrated safe success rates that significantly outperform conventional methods.
contributions: Proposed CS-Pi, an inference-time constraint-satisfying sampler that loops projection onto safe constraints with adaptive renoising scaled to the projection residual.
Avoided inaccurate gradient approximations (proxies) on noisy intermediate states altogether, operating only on clean actions to reliably switch between modes in multimodal policies.
Extended the formulation to continuous costs (soft constraints) such as orientation preferences by simply replacing the projection step with a proximal operator.

Demonstrated safe success rates significantly superior to existing gradient guidance and projection baselines across simulated environments (2D avoidance, 7-DoF shelf picking, orientation control) and a physical Franka robot.

sections.heading: Balancing Safety and Plausibility: Why Existing Test-Time Control Fails
sections.summary: Satisfying unseen safety constraints at test time requires not only entering the safe set, but also maintaining natural, plausible actions that accomplish the task. Traditional gradient guidance easily breaks down due to approximations at noisy stages, while naive projection strays out-of-distribution and fails the task. CS-Pi resolves this challenge by combining projection and renoising.
sections.details:
Flow-matching policies pretrained on large demonstration datasets can perform diverse tasks like object manipulation and folding clothes. But in the field, novel safety constraints suddenly arise, such as avoiding an unfamiliar wine glass. The goal here is to balance safety—satisfying the constraint—with plausibility, remaining an action the policy is likely to generate to complete the task. Forcibly avoiding the glass is useless if the gripper lets go of the drawer handle and fails the task.

Mainstream gradient guidance suffers from two main weaknesses. First, on/off hard constraints (like collision vs. non-collision) do not have gradients, forcing the use of smooth penalty functions that cannot strictly guarantee safety. Second, because guidance acts on intermediate noisy states, it calculates cost gradients on a proxy: the expected value of the clean action. If the policy is uncertain between passing left or right of an obstacle, that expectation passes right through the center of the obstacle, sending the gradient in a completely unhelpful direction.

Classical rejection sampling selects directly from the policy's outputs, keeping actions plausible, but waiting for a safe draw is intractable when safe actions are rare. On the other hand, projection quickly moves an action to the nearest safe set, but often causes jerky motions or loses task intent. The authors' key insight is using flow-matching generation to fuse both approaches. Instead of executing the projected action directly, CS-Pi adds noise scaled to the projection distance and denoises again with the policy. This efficiently pulls the action toward regions that are both safe and highly plausible under the policy.

captions.F2: Comparison of sampling methods. Gradient guidance (left) derails trajectories due to inaccurate proxy gradients; projection (mid-left) yields unnatural, out-of-distribution actions; rejection sampling (mid-right) requires impractically many redraws. The proposed CS-Pi (right) adaptively renoises based on the projection residual $\delta$ and re-runs the policy, reaching the safe set efficiently and plausibly.

sections.heading: Related Work and How CS-Pi Fits In
sections.summary: Inference-time control for diffusion and flow models includes gradient guidance, particle filters, control barrier functions (CBF), and partial renoising. However, each suffers from failures in multimodal distributions, unnatural out-of-distribution behaviors, or excessive computational cost. CS-Pi neatly integrates their respective strengths.
sections.details:
### Limitations of Gradient Guidance
Gradient guidance, widely used in Diffuser and various diffusion models, relies on intermediate noisy predictions (proxies). It breaks down when costs have high curvature or when distributions are multimodal. Attempts like Trust Sampling try to restrict trust regions, yet still depend on proxy gradients.

### Rejection, Weighting, and Projection Approaches
Rejection sampling and sequential Monte Carlo (SMC) evaluate actions post-generation, preserving plausibility. However, they demand massive computation (particle counts) when the safe set is small. Conversely, directly projecting actions onto the safe set is fast, but ignores the policy's learned distribution and disrupts motion. CS-Pi uses projection not as the final output, but as an anchor for the next sample, achieving both efficiency and plausibility.

### Differences from Control Barrier Function (CBF) Samplers
CBF-based methods such as SafeDiffuser and SafeFlowMatcher provide theoretical safety guarantees, but do not guarantee plausibility. Because they continuously deform the current trajectory, they cannot perform a mode switch to an alternate route when blocked by an obstacle. They also require differentiable barrier functions. CS-Pi only requires solving a projection onto the safe set and can hop to an alternative route when necessary.

### Advancing Partial Renoising
Partial renoising, known from image editing (e.g., SDEdit), adds a small amount of noise and denoises again. Previously, this was applied just once with a manually tuned noise level on human sketches. CS-Pi is novel in applying this loop to the robot policy's own outputs, automatically adapting the noise level according to the projection distance.

sections.heading: How CS-Pi Works: The Draw-Project-Renoise Loop and Cost Extensions
sections.summary: CS-Pi is a simple algorithm repeating a draw $\to$ project $\to$ renoise $\to$ denoise loop. It automatically tunes the noise level based on the projection distance, refining the action until it enters the safe set. Using proximal operators, it also optimizes continuous costs.
sections.details:
### The Draw-Project-Renoise Algorithm
A flow-matching policy $\pi_\theta$ generates a clean action $\mathbf{a}$ by solving an ODE starting from standard Gaussian noise $\mathbf{a}_0$. CS-Pi begins by drawing an initial candidate action $\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)}$ as usual.
- **Projection Step**: Project the action to the nearest point on the safe set $\mathcal{C}$, denoted $\mathbf{a}_c^{(i)} = \mathcal{P}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)})$. This point acts as an anchor.
- **Residual Calculation**: Compute the projection residual $\delta^{(i)} = \|\hat{\mathbf{a}}^{(i)} - \mathbf{a}_c^{(i)}\|$.
- **Adaptive Noise Level**: If the residual is small, the action is nearly safe, so only a little noise is added; if large, substantial noise is added to explore an entirely different route. Specifically, the intermediate time is set to $n^{(i)} = k / (k + \delta^{(i)})$ using a hyperparameter $k$.
- **Renoise and Redraw**: Add noise to the anchor to form the state at time $n^{(i)}$, $\mathbf{a}_n^{(i)} = n^{(i)} \mathbf{a}_c^{(i)} + (1 - n^{(i)}) \bm{\epsilon}$. From here, solve the ODE with the unmodified policy $\pi_\theta$ to draw the next candidate action.

This loop repeats until the action lies within the safe set (residual $\delta \le \tau$). On average, the residual shrinks with each iteration, converging to an action that is both safe and plausible.

### Extending to Soft Preferences (Continuous Costs)
Beyond hard obstacles, tasks often have soft preferences, such as keeping the gripper vertical while carrying a cup. In CS-Pi, replacing the projection step $\mathcal{P}$ with a proximal operator $\mathrm{prox}_{\beta L}(\hat{\mathbf{a}}) = \arg\min_{\mathbf{a}} [L(\mathbf{a}) + \frac{1}{2\beta}\|\mathbf{a} - \hat{\mathbf{a}}\|^2]$ allows running the exact same loop. Furthermore, sequencing a proximal step followed by a projection onto a hard constraint enables prioritized constraint composition in an exceptionally simple manner.

### Terminal Projection
If the maximum number of iterations $K_{\max}$ is reached without entering the safe set, CS-Pi offers the option to apply a single forced projection to the final action to strictly prioritize safety. Because the loop has already pulled the action very close to the safe set, this preserves far more plausibility than a one-shot projection from scratch.

sections.heading: Simulations and Hardware Experiments: High Safety while Retaining Plausibility
sections.summary: Evaluations spanned 2D navigation, a 7-DoF shelf pick-and-place, orientation-constrained reaching, and zero-shot deployment on a physical Franka robot. CS-Pi achieved an 81.3% safe success rate on the shelf task and 55% on hardware, markedly outperforming gradient and projection baselines.
sections.details:
### 4.1 2D Avoidance: Satisfying Constraints Without Breaking Distribution
In a multimodal 2D planar navigation task across 6 obstacle scenarios unseen during training, CS-Pi achieved a 99.0% safe success rate. It retained 85.7% of all waypoints within the demonstration support and recorded the highest log-likelihood at 1.53, showing superior plausibility. Simple projection achieved 99.7% safety but catastrophic plausibility (log-likelihood of -85.89), while gradient guidance reached only a 67.2% success rate.

### 4.2 Shelf Pick-and-Place: Preserving Task Semantics
A 7-DoF robot grasps a cube from a 3-tier shelf and places it on a table, facing newly introduced obstacles at test time. For safe success (avoiding collisions and completing both pick and place), gradient guidance reached 32.0% and projection scored 55.3%, whereas CS-Pi achieved 81.3%. Baselines pushed the arm away from the obstacle but also away from the cube, missing the grasp; CS-Pi regenerated motions that weaved around obstacles directly to the cube.

### 4.3 3D-Orient: Reaching under Orientation Preferences
In reaching for a target while keeping the end-effector pointing vertically downward, inverse kinematics redundancy causes gradient guidance to fail (under 6.7% success) because the proxy averages multiple distinct solutions. In contrast, CS-Pi with a proximal operator achieved a 98.9% reach rate and a 65.6% overall success rate.

### 4.4 Real Robot Validation (Franka FR3)
Using an external RGB-D camera to detect obstacle bounding boxes, the pretrained large model $\pi_{0.5}$ was deployed zero-shot without fine-tuning. In an apple pick-and-place task onto a blue plate, CS-Pi achieved an average safe success rate of 55%, well above projection (40%), gradient guidance (25%), and Trust Sampling (20%). It maintained practical speed with a per-step latency of 0.143 seconds.

sections.heading: Conclusion: Gaining Safety Without Sacrificing Pretrained Policy Value
sections.summary: CS-Pi achieves safe and plausible sampling strictly at inference time through an alternating projection and renoising loop. Eliminating fragile gradient estimates on noisy states, it delivers high safety and task success on real hardware, opening a practical path to field-adapting robots without retraining.
sections.details:
CS-Pi provides a robust framework for sampling safe, plausible actions from flow-matching policies. At its core is a straightforward loop: project the generated action, re-add noise scaled to the displacement, and run the policy again.

It completely eliminates inaccurate gradient proxies on intermediate noisy states and requires no extra neural network training. Through proximal operators, it smoothly extends to optimizing continuous costs. Across simulations and real hardware experiments, it proved to be the only sampler capable of satisfying constraints while preserving the intelligent behaviors originally learned by the policy. This represents a highly practical breakthrough for adapting foundation models to varied real-world safety requirements without costly retraining.

sections.heading: Appendix: Theoretical Insights and Failure Mechanisms
sections.summary: The appendix details why gradient guidance fails on multimodal distributions due to Jensen's inequality and proxy divergence. It also proves that a single CS-Pi iteration is equivalent to Gaussian window filtering and verifies mode-switching capabilities when one path is blocked.
sections.details:
### Why Gradient Guidance Fails (App. E)
At noisy state $a_t$, the ideal guidance direction is the expected cost gradient across the clean action posterior: $\mathbb{E}[\nabla L(a_1) \mid a_t]$. Because this expectation is intractable, existing gradient guidance methods substitute it with $\nabla L(\mathbb{E}[a_1 \mid a_t])$—the gradient of the expectation (a Jensen's swap). When the posterior is multimodal, the expectation $\mathbb{E}[a_1 \mid a_t]$ lies midway between modes (e.g., straight inside the obstacle), yielding garbage gradients that point toward neither valid avoidance route.

### Single-Iteration Sampling Rule (App. F)
Theoretical analysis proves that one step of CS-Pi's renoise-and-denoise process is mathematically equivalent to sampling from the original policy $\pi_\theta$ filtered by a Gaussian window centered at the anchor with standard deviation $\sigma = \delta / k$.

### Escaping Blocked Modes (App. M)
In an experiment with a bimodal Gaussian mixture where one mode is completely blocked by an obstacle, simple projection and CBF samplers (like SafeDiffuser) made only deterministic adjustments around the blocked mode, failing to switch to the remaining mode (0% transition rate). In contrast, CS-Pi successfully hopped to the safe alternate mode 85.9% of the time.

takeaways: In test-time guidance for diffusion and flow models, computing gradients on intermediate noisy proxies causes catastrophic failure in multimodal settings; pairing clean-space corrections with renoising is far more effective.
Using the projection displacement (residual $\delta$) as an indicator of uncertainty to adapt the noise schedule keeps hyperparameter tuning to a minimum (essentially just $k$).
Hard geometric constraints (obstacles) and soft task preferences (end-effector orientation) can be handled in a unified, prioritized manner by sequencing proximal operators and projections.
Real-world deployments can satisfy bounding-box constraints from external vision pipelines (like SAM 2 and depth) zero-shot, without retraining foundation models such as VLAs.
limitations: While individual iterations are theoretically characterized, a mathematical proof guaranteeing that the overall projection-renoise loop always converges to a safe solution remains an open question.
The approach relies on having fast projection operators (or proximal operators); non-convex, highly complex constraint sets could introduce solver latency or local minima issues.

Because sampling operates myopically on action chunks (short, fixed-length action sequences), it cannot prevent global planning failures where an action chunk successfully avoids a local obstacle only to enter a dead end.
